analysis.one_liner: Bars financial regulators from working on matters involving their former employers or clients, and restricts the revolving door.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in three House committees and two subcommittees until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targets the 'revolving door' — the movement of officials between government financial-regulatory jobs and the industry they oversee. It would ban federal employees from collecting bonuses or severance from private firms tied to taking a government job, require senior officials at agencies like the Federal Reserve, SEC, and FDIC to step aside from any matter benefiting their recent former employer or client, bar officials from working on matters involving companies they are negotiating a future job with, and block former regulators from lobbying the government for two years after leaving. It also tightens rules for government contract procurement and adds criminal and civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary bank customers, investors, and taxpayers, who depend on financial regulators deciding cases on the merits rather than with an eye toward a future industry job. Public-integrity groups and honest regulators also benefit from clearer rules.

how_it_helps.text: Requires senior financial-services regulators to recuse from any official action giving a direct, substantial financial benefit to a former employer or client from the previous two years, with waivers allowed only in writing and posted publicly [S3].
Prohibits regulators from participating in matters involving a firm they are negotiating future employment with, and requires them to disclose job negotiations to their agency's ethics official [S3].

Amends federal criminal law so that bonuses, severance, and retention payments contingent on taking a government job count as illegal compensation, closing a path by which private firms effectively pre-pay future officials [S3].

Bars former senior financial regulators from lobbying the executive branch or Congress for two years after leaving, and doubles the existing one-year cooling-off period for bank examiners to two years [S3].

Bars federal employees from working on contract awards for a contractor that employed them within the prior two years, and extends the ban on former procurement officials taking contractor pay to two years, covering affiliates and subcontractors [S3].
Enforces these rules with criminal penalties up to five years for willful violations and civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation or the amount of compensation involved [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large banks, securities firms, and other financial companies lose a hiring pipeline that lets them place alumni inside the agencies regulating them; lobbying and law firms lose the supply of former regulators who can sell access; and government contractors lose ready access to former procurement officials.

drawbacks.text: The pay restrictions could make recruiting harder: banks can no longer offer retention bonuses or severance to induce executives into government service, and the two-year lobbying ban could shrink the pool of experienced people willing to take senior regulatory jobs at lower government pay [S3].

Broad recusal requirements can slow agency work — a regulator with an industry background may have to step aside from many routine matters, leaving decisions to less-informed staff, though the bill allows agency heads to grant written waivers in the public interest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but modest: stricter ethics rules can make recruiting experienced industry professionals into government somewhat harder and can occasionally force recusals, but the bill builds in written, publicly posted waivers for cases where the restrictions would obstruct the work. Against that, the bill addresses a structural problem — regulators deciding issues that directly affect the firms they came from or hope to join — that existing rules handle only loosely. The design is reasonably careful rather than badly designed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to two Judiciary subcommittees, and none of them ever scheduled a hearing or markup, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Elijah Cummings introduced the bill on February 3, 2017, early in the new Congress [S1].
The Speaker referred it to the Committees on Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary, and Financial Services [S5].

On March 2, 2017, it was referred to the Judiciary subcommittees on the Constitution and Civil Justice and on Crime, Terrorism, Homeland Security, and Investigations; that was the last action ever taken [S5].
Only one other member cosponsored the bill, and it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial firms, lobbying shops, and contractors keep the existing revolving door: they can still pay future officials bonuses for joining government, place alumni inside regulators, and hire regulators right after they leave. Committee leadership was never forced to take a position.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial firms and the revolving door

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Democrats, and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.note: The bill would bar senior regulators from acting on matters benefiting their recent former employers or clients, and bar regulators negotiating jobs from related matters — cutting off a channel by which banks gain influence inside their own regulators. Banks keep that advantage because the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Lobbying and law firms serving financial clients
industries.note: A two-year lobbying ban on former senior financial regulators, plus recusal and disclosure rules, would reduce the supply of well-connected former officials firms can sell to clients. The ban never took effect.

The bill would double to two years the ban on former procurement officials taking contractor pay, extend it to affiliates and subcontractors, and bar employees from working on contracts for their former contractor employer. Contractors retain current looser rules.
